notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0040.stoa061c.opp-l: Line 1: 'taus' read as 'laus'. Line 4: 'Deo proximam' read as 'Deo proximant' (draw near to God). Line 5: 'aversos respicit nutantes, quos integros videre nequivit' is obscure; translated literally, possibly referring to double or swaying vision. Line 6: 'Dolor enim amissi innueris s ne vini quavis nimietate' is corrupt; read as 'amissi funeris vini quavis nimietate' (grief for one lost cannot be tempered by any excess of wine); if 's ne' is 'sine', the sense would be inverted. 'abstinete vos tali.. agentes' is also damaged. Luke reference printed as XXI, 3i, read as 21:34. The servant beaten with many stripes alludes to Luke 12:45-47.

Line 7: 'in serviles indurata amores' is odd ('hardened into base/servile loves'); the text may be corrupt. 'nihil legis ducere' read as 'docere' (teach). 'ut eas magis idiae' read as 'viduae' (widows). The clause after 'tantum caveat jurare' ('de his quae egerit... juramenta persolvere') is marked doubtful by the edition and its syntax is unclear; rendered literally with a gap. 'prostituta ad luxuriari alios' is garbled; rendered by sense. Line 8: 'Cathinis' read as 'catinis' (dishes), uncertain; 'persinis' taken as 'persicis/purple' colours, uncertain. 'ab infantibus contumeliis' read as 'infandis'; 'corruptionem' read as 'correptionem' (correction). 'de omnibus se habentibus vocem' is obscure. Scriptural references printed in the edition are given as printed, with evident scanning errors corrected.

Line 10: the Romans reference printed as 'II, 5' is corrected to 2:3 per the quoted verse. Lines ab1–12 are the Maurist editors' prefatory note to the following work (De vera et falsa poenitentia), not part of De sobrietate. Line 11: 'dist. Ii' read as dist. 2; 'capp. 33 ct 54' read as 33 and 34; 'vulgari ruta' read as vulgata. 'Meliori quam potest confiteatur' is elliptical; rendered 'to a better [priest] than he can'. In line 12 'omissu ad Christi devotam' is obscure, probably 'omisso: Ad Christi devotam', i.e. a dedicatory phrase omitted; uncertain.

nodes.text: ON SOBRIETY AND CHASTITY, ONE BOOK, BY AN UNCERTAIN AUTHOR.

CHAPTER ONE. Three vices to be avoided. The praise of sobriety. The evils of drunkenness. The use of wine. What it is useful for. Why it is forbidden to priests. The harms of drunkenness. The Scriptures by which this vice is condemned. Surfeit is pressed on mourners by their friends at funerals. Drunkenness is hostile to body and soul. Since the changeable mind of mortals takes delight sometimes in good intentions and sometimes in bad, and many are carried headlong either by repentance for evil deeds to good acts, or by sluggishness of mind from good acts to bad, they give rise to matters for discussion for those who weigh morals: when these are recognised, the corrected may rejoice, while the unconverted are put to shame in their wicked ways. For you would more easily find people who abandon evil than people who seek the good, because to very many, indeed to almost all mortals, the things that pamper the flesh are sweeter than those that rein it in from vices. And since the advantages of the pursuit of honourable conduct are to be urged by us, we warn anyone who wishes to serve as a soldier in such a resolve that he must not be sluggish, sleepy, or drunk: for unless a person has turned aside from these three vices, he can never be secure or safe; rather, he will always be exposed to every danger, and even to death itself. For strength overpowers the enemy, watchfulness thwarts those who lay ambushes, and sobriety makes a person's heart prepared. For this reason the Lord our God, with fatherly affection, has commanded us through his Prophets and Apostles to abstain utterly from all vices, and above all from drunkenness, which is the whirlpool of all vices. About the evil of this vice we wish to set out some things for the reader, whom we urge only to apply an attentive mind to our admonitions and to pardon our discourse, even if it is less brilliant than the ear of the eloquent demands. For we urge our hearers to attend to the reasoning of what is said, and not to expect the gloss of frothy speech or artful eloquence. Therefore first, for the sake of the title and dignity of this little book, let us set out as far as we can the fruits and benefits of sobriety; and afterwards let us make known the unseemly troubles of drunkenness.

For sobriety is chastity of sense and mind, the protection of all the limbs and of the body, the bulwark of chastity and modesty, next neighbour to shame, keeper of friendship and peace, always joined to honour, a fugitive from all crimes and vices, steadfast in right judgement, wisdom inseparable from memory and recollection, guardian of secrets, veil of hidden things, capable of reading and learning, at once pupil and teacher of studies and good arts, attendant on minds that are to be won, always eager for good repute, producing wholesome and useful things in the thoughts, a singular aid to virtue, arranging all things with reason, always presenting itself in the company of honourable people. Sobriety flees rashness, avoids all dangers, complies with mutual duties, detests pride, governs house and household with moderation, keeps faith with those who entrust themselves to it; and, to speak summarily and briefly, perseverance in sobriety is an inestimable strength of soul: all the virtues and all titles of praise always desire it, because without it they cannot be adorned or give pleasure.

Drunkenness, on the contrary, begins with injury to the soul, and is the mother of all shameful deeds, the material of faults, the root of crimes, the origin of all vices, the disturbance of the head, the overthrow of the senses, a storm of the tongue, a tempest of the body, the shipwreck of chastity. Drunkenness is the loss of time, voluntary madness, disgraceful languor, the weakening of a sound mind, foulness of character, the disgrace of life, the dishonour of decency, the corruption of the soul. Drunkenness, as we see daily, brings down very many members of great families, and, leaving them bereft of care in management, makes them sell off for a paltry coin what their parents and grandparents had gathered well and long and acquired at enormous price. Drunkenness in both sexes always seeks every evil and commits abominations. Drunkenness takes away the fear of God and removes the future judgement of God from the hearts of those who have it. Drunkenness, says the Apostle, denies the heavenly kingdom to those who seek it (1 Cor. 6:10). Drunkenness steals time from the drunk and filches the days; it does not remember what was entrusted to it, and does not look, with mind or eyes, at what is set before it. From a servant it not only takes away faithfulness, but also makes him useless, through frauds, for the duty of service; and [there are] other evils that cannot be comprehended.

And since by some people the use of wine is not moderated, but rather excess is sought, both danger to bodily condition and to life, and very grave damage to reputation and good name are incurred. For the gift of wine was provided for bodily remedies; to those who abuse it, it is utterly forbidden, and the discipline of sobriety is ordained to be kept. Wine is indeed necessary in many [circumstances] of mortal life: it restores a weak stomach, repairs failing strength, warms one who is chilled with cold, heals wounds when poured on them, and, joined to antidotes and various medicines, produces health; it removes sadness, wipes out all languor of the soul, pours in gladness, and makes guests engage in honourable conversation: but taken a little too freely, it is in a certain way turned into poison for the drinker. For this reason we read that abstinence from wine was commanded by the Lord first to the priests and Levites, because it was fitting that those should first undertake to observe the measure of sobriety who were to hand on the divine precepts to be observed by the rest of mortals, not by words but by deeds, and fulfil them with habits of chastity and holiness, as the book of Leviticus says: And he said to Aaron, Wine and anything that can make drunk you shall not drink, you and your sons, when you enter the tabernacle of the testimony, lest you die: for it is an everlasting precept in your generations (Lev. 10:9). The prophet Ezekiel also says likewise: And no priest shall drink wine when he begins to enter the inner court (Ezek. 44:21). Very many secular authors, indeed, have published precepts of sobriety in many books; we do not bring forward their assertions against the vices of drunkenness, because it is fitting that human things be confirmed by divine testimonies, not divine things by human ones. Therefore sobriety ought, with fitting observance, to vie with the priestly disposition: for whoever approaches the altar of the divine majesty not sober will experience the destruction of an untimely death. For whoever, endowed with the priestly honour, is close to drunkenness, is near to punishment. And against those who draw near to God, if they are drunk, the punishments that rage are not far off. Therefore whoever, appointed priest by divine gift, approaches the celebration of the sacrament drunk, has no delay of the death that will follow. For excess is always contrary to everything: and in whichever sex immoderation is applied, it produces vice. Therefore whatever is immoderate and undisciplined meets a fall close to ruin; for where there is no measure, all is danger: whatever thing lacks moderation hurls itself into destruction.

Thus, then, when someone immoderate, in the middle of a banquet, having lost the reins of restraint, has been laid low by insane drunkenness, he sees things turned away and swaying, which he could not see whole, or in long talk pours out superfluous words and composes empty sayings, shouting badly yet sounding fine to himself; with downcast face he lies back on his couch, vomiting and wholly unaware of himself, and makes a spectacle for the banquet: and while nothing sound comes of him, with nothing else compelling him but wine, he lays open the secrets of his heart, and brings out into the open the secrets his friends entrusted to him. He is found ready to commit every crime of cruelty or foulness, he whom no reasoning of a sober mind, but drunkenness, rules. Among the cups he takes up unjust quarrels, and with no cause at all stirs up a bitter brawl: for by thrusting in empty words he does not allow others' sound sayings, and he rises up to insult the guests and [to charge] the crimes of his neighbours.

That you, reader, may receive these things willingly, I thought you should be admonished. Therefore read carefully the epistle of the apostle Peter to the Gentiles, [the epistles] of Paul to the Romans, the first to the Corinthians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, and to Titus. Moreover, to guard against drunkenness, hear our Lord Jesus Christ saying in the Gospel: Take heed to yourselves, he says, lest perhaps your hearts be weighed down with surfeit and drunkenness (Luke 21:34). And the Lord is angry with the servant, on whom he threatens to inflict many stripes at his coming. Therefore abstain, you who act or do such things; abstain from your madness, and recognise yourselves as humane human beings, and cast such great foulness away from you, and avoid the crimes of drunkenness with all your strength. Mark a saying that is rustic, but sound: Wine is a medicine; taken more than is right, it is known to be poison. Cast such great foulness away from you, then, and avoid the crimes of drunkenness with all your strength. The nature of wine was created for gladness, not for drunkenness (Sir. 31:35), so that by its moderate use thirst may be quenched, yet not so that it is drunk to the point of drunkenness. Flee surfeit, speaking or doing [only] those things at which the sober need not blush. Flee the surfeit that is pressed upon those who are already mourning enough, by consoling friends or relatives at funerals. For the grief of a lost loved one cannot be tempered by any excess of wine. But you, O man in good health, daily long to vomit under the compulsion of wine: and you are filled with as much as would let very many rejoice with gladness and be soberly satisfied. Do you not consider it shameful that a man should pour into himself more wine than he holds, and not know the measure of his own stomach? Do you not consider that one bound fast by drunkenness cannot be in his own power? Why do you go to excess in drinking, except to grow more insolent, for the worse, through the provocation of wine? From this misery of drinking there arises a disgraceful contest between those challenged and those challenging, and for the winner the disgrace is worse. From this, indeed, the limbs of many refuse food and, given over to wine, waste away in premature debility and unripe old age, and while still green in years they are shaken with a trembling quiver. Hence the lungs rot with the daily burning of wine, and through their mouths, as of the dead, they send out foul breath. In such people, then, there is no reason, no plan for conducting life, no memory of things done or read, nor any foresight of arts or industry: since the setting of the sun sees such a man reclining at lunch, and the unexpected day overtakes him spending the night at dinner, and while in continual madness, reclining day and night, he dozes or drinks, he is buried daily while still placed in this life.

CHAPTER II. The Lord's virgins are instructed in rules. Funeral vigils. But what am I to say now, or what am I to keep silent? If, then, any of this drunkenness has befallen women, [the drunkenness] which has loaded the male sex with the masses of crimes touched on above, nothing must be kept silent; rather, we must labour so that this divine admonition may correct those women who are such, and that sobriety, through fear of correction, may restrain [them] from drunkenness. But since we began the work of this little book by admonishing men, starting from priests and levites or ministers, it is right and fitting that in admonishing the female sex we make our beginning from the Lord's holy virgins: so that in general every rank and sex may be held without excuse by this admonition. The Lord's virgin ought to recognise which precepts it befits her to hold to, and from how many vices she ought to abstain, if she wishes both to reign with God while placed in the world, and to reign with him in heavenly glory after the dissolution of this life. The Lord's virgin ought first of all to avoid being seen in public and to shun the crowds of the streets, and, staying at home, to devote herself to wool-working or to divine reading. Lord's virgin, when you sit or stand in a gathering of lay women, do not give their scurrilous or lewd words or songs the benefit of your presence; but rather flee, shut your eyes and ears: lest, deprived of the fear of God, you let into your senses devilish thoughts by which you may perhaps perish in a short time. Let the Lord's virgin go forth neither with adornment of the head, nor with styling of the hair, nor with eyes raised or merry, but with her face lowered to the ground: lest, hardened into base loves, she become a cause of perdition to others, even if she herself does not perish. For how many deaths of the soul the desire of the eyes brings about, the voice of the Gospel declares to us (Matt. 5:29). The Lord's virgin ought to abstain entirely from every shameless speech or laughter, and to adorn her whole life with silence and discipline. The Lord's virgin who has stained her face with some cosmetic for the brightness of her cheeks will dread the sentence pronounced in the prophet Isaiah upon the daughters of Zion (Isa. 3:16-17). The Lord's virgin, as the Apostle teaches concerning widows, if she is chattering in speech, or wordy in talkativeness, or excessively curious, cannot be judged chaste (1 Tim. 5:13); rather, as one prostituted, she inflames others the more to wantonness. Lord's virgin, do not entrust yourself to any man, of whatever age, in a private dwelling or conversation without the presence of very grave women: and when you are staying alone in your lodging, sit with the doors closed behind you, and do not readily open your door to any man who knocks; lest perhaps you fall into the foulest suspicion, or into the shipwreck of your modesty. The Lord's virgin ought not to go to places where men sleep, lest she be believed to have offered herself like a harlot to her corruptors. Lord's virgin, shun the company and conversation of a woman who teaches evil and lives a wretched life, or who has at some time been troubled by ill repute: since the apostle Paul teaches that good morals are corrupted by evil conversations (1 Cor. 15:33). The Lord's virgin, in order to extinguish the flames of lust and of all wantonness, ought to give herself to fasting and abstinence, and to persist in prayers day and night, if she desires both to escape the snares and ambushes of the lurking devil and to arrive at the promised rewards of virginity. Lord's virgin, flee utterly from every brother whom bad report marks out as one to be avoided, and as far as you can keep your approaches away from him and from his banquets. Let the Lord's virgin not be unaware that from table conversation the vices of lust grow up, and from there one comes to the sins of fornication. The Lord's virgin, to conclude quickly, ought to abstain from all the allurements of gluttony, and ought to be content with sparing food and drink, and always adorned with honourable silence. It is the gift of God to the Lord's virgin not to know how to be angry, but rather to know how to restrain anger; to be kind to all; not to make signs with her eyes; not to frame her tongue with deceit and malice; neither to eavesdrop on nor to betray the secrets of another's house; to flee avarice and greed; not to deny deposits entrusted to her; not to put money out at interest; to forgive a sister's fault from the heart; to place a stumbling-block before no one; to offer consolation to the afflicted; to minister to the sick; not to agree with one who disparages another, but to abstain wholly from disparagement. That the Lord's virgin ought to stand in silence in church and teach nothing of the law, hear the Apostle saying: Let women keep silent in church; it is shameful for women to speak in church. Likewise he says: Let women learn in silence. Likewise: I do not permit women to teach (1 Cor. 14:34-35; 1 Tim. 2:11-12). If, then, it is shameful for women to teach or to speak in church, how much more for virgins, whom the care and profession of chastity promised to God binds, so that widows rather may imitate them in good works? Let the Lord's virgin say nothing perverse or scurrilous or feigned, and let her root out lying entirely from her mouth. For the Lord will destroy those who speak lies, as David teaches in the fifth psalm, and his son in the book of Wisdom (Ps. 5:7; Wis. 1:11). As much good faith as the Lord's virgin ought to show in all things, so much let her beware of swearing: [...] to discharge oaths about what she has done for the sake of confirming the truth. Let her recognise the Lord forewarning in the Gospel that she should not swear at all or in any way (Matt. 5:34). Let the Lord's virgin beware of committing thefts and frauds, or bearing false witness, or consenting to those who do these things: for blessed Paul rebukes those who commit them (1 Cor. 6:8; Rom. 1:32). Let the Lord's virgin avoid being present at married women's banquets at which men mingle, lest men talking with her among the cups bring upon her the sin of concupiscence. Lord's virgin, against all sounds produced by the art of music, against all worldly songs, against everything that is sweetly pleasing to hear, close your ears and your heart: lest the devil's melody cut the love of Christ from her heart. Lord's virgin, turn your face away, as far as you can, from the movements and bendings of dancers, of women cymbal-players or drum-players, and of all male entertainments: lest, struck by the sudden dart of love for any of them, you begin grievously to perish. Let the Lord's virgin not only beware lest she be proud or quarrelsome, but also withdraw far, as far as she can, from the proud and the quarrelsome: For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble, as Solomon cries in the Proverbs (Prov. 29:23). The Lord's virgin ought not to exalt herself by boastful speech, nor by riches, nor by nobility of birth; but she ought to remain, as long as she lives, in the humility and poverty of spirit acceptable to Christ. For in the judgement of God it is not these things but one's own acts that will be weighed, from which each will receive a reward according to how they have acted, not according to how they were born. The Lord's virgin ought to shun funeral vigils and the other [gatherings] that take place in private houses, especially where people gather mingled without distinction of sex. The Lord's virgin who, according to her means, gives nothing cannot be called or believed a handmaid of God. But, to speak briefly, the Lord's virgin who strives to keep the guard of her modesty promised to the Lord ought not to sin at all, neither by conspicuous gait, nor by soft gesture or word, nor by idleness of speech, nor in body, nor in mind.

CHAPTER III. The crimes of drink in virgins or women. The evils of drunkenness are touched on in general. Why the author began with priests. And since we may believe that what has been said in admonishing holy virgins can suffice, from which precepts it befits also the servants of God and all lay people to observe [what applies to them], we ought now to come to enumerating the crimes of drink, and to show that drunkenness surpasses all vices. First, for virgins themselves, drunkenness does not allow them to fulfil the promises of chastity; for it has always been hostile to holy pledges in both sexes: and therefore drunkenness cannot be the companion of modesty, since chastity was never the ally of intoxication. Sobriety in women lowers the gaze to the ground; but drunkenness, modesty lost, raises a shameless face. For sobriety, with the greatest trepidation, utters a blameless word, and with silence one fitting [to the occasion]; drunkenness makes both a woman's speech and her face shameless. For drunkenness draws out and wrings from her an unspeakable, shameless voice about all her affairs, and she into whom excess of wine has crept through greed can have no shame to keep silent: from which intoxication follows weakness of the limbs. And so it happens that, just as a ship dashed upon a rock by the waves of a mighty sea is shattered, so a woman's body and mind, dashed by a great storm of wine, are dissolved in all their limbs. For she who by nature cannot plant firm footsteps when walking, how will she be able to go along when struck by a huge storm of wine, with slipping step and nodding, always with rolling eyes, leaning back or with drooping neck, a maidservant attendant guiding her because of the fault of her intoxication? There is no soundness there, and no care of the house or governing of the household; the stammering tongue is deprived of the office of speech, or, wishing to burst into speech, it is not only not understood but even laughed at by those who hear. She is out of her mind and wholly unaware of herself; her headdress slips to one side and shows her half-bare neck to onlookers, and, dishevelled on every side, she is a cause of blushing to those who look at her, and she does not know what is done at home. In such a woman modesty is without doubt endangered, and every secret that sobriety guards in women, intoxication makes public. When she has been seized by dizziness on the ground and laid out on her bed, she sees all the walls running round her: she thinks the roof of the house is stretched at the bottom and the bottom on high, and she is taken up as though buried in sleep. As for the bedding, which is befouled with unspeakable defilements, the intoxication of such a mistress is mocked by all the women and maidservants with laughter no longer hidden but open. And so, as time passes and the vice of drunkenness remains, all fear flies from her heart: she does not think of the correction, or the terror, or the force of a husband who often rebukes her. Hence the house, neglected daily as time slips by, is so stripped of its daily order that the husband always wishes for death, whose labour and management under such a mistress daily diminish and come to ruin. There is no one with whom he may confer about the care of the house, so that something may be arranged for the better: since, of course, she shows only the name of a wife, not the character. With her arranging nothing, the husband's daily care is worn out, not without sadness: for as with oxen yoked to a wagon, if one ceases to strain under the load, the other's effort will burst him. So, the mistress being drunk and the keys of the rooms taken away, everything is tampered with: the fullness of the storerooms is emptied daily by servants' thefts, and the whole house resounds with the clamour of an undisciplined household. The care of wool-work becomes either negligent, or nonexistent, or loathsome. For to such a mistress the maid who has offered a larger cup will be dearer and more lovable than the one who has handed in a complete task of spinning before evening. For she delights in dishes and in various and purple colours in wine, not in tunics: and she seeks to have brought to her not the measure of clothes to be made, but of wine. She does not set up looms for weaving for the sake of guarding chastity, she who long ago lost the use of the loom from her house through drunkenness: and the webs she took away from idle maids she has given to spiders to weave. When she takes food, she scarcely touches half an ounce of bread in eating, and then swallows cups, and for that reason seeks relishes as poultices for herself. As long as she is awake, she drinks: or if she falls asleep, thirst breaks off her sleep. But why do I linger further? If I wished to recount all the vices of drunkenness, time would fail me before [I finished]: since the Holy Spirit cries out weightier things in Solomon's Ecclesiasticus, saying: A drunken woman is a great anger, and her disgrace and shame will not be covered. And of both sexes he says: Wine destroys many. And again: Drunkenness swallows up prudence. And again: Wine drunk to excess causes provocations and angers and many ruins. Wine drunk to excess is bitterness of the soul (Ecclus. 26:11; 31:30, 38 and 39).

Therefore, to make an end of the book, I will touch on everything briefly. For through wine chastity has been drowned; and very many crowds have been deceived by seducers. Many virgins too, driven by wine and forgetful of the marriage bed, have handed over their modesty to adulterers, and have made pacts with lovers for the death of their husbands. Very many, driven headlong by wine, have defiled themselves in indecent gatherings: and by fathers or mothers, by sons or daughters, by brothers or sisters, by sons-in-law or daughters-in-law, through unspeakable unions, as has been said, have begotten children for themselves. For through drink very many men and very many women have fallen from a holy and pious resolve, and, forgetful of themselves, having lost their honours, have remained without standing: and, fugitives from their ancestral homes, they have ended their life not where they received it. Through this same wine the strong have been struck down by the weak, and very many laid low in death by a woman's blow: and unconquered armies, with wine in control, have been wiped out and subdued under the yoke of slavery. Countless men who long refused the yoke of domination, drink has brought under another's will. Through the habit of wine very many have been turned to madness; and, as the madness of mind persisted, separated from human company, they have mostly been devoured by the tooth of wild beasts. The immoderate excess of wine has made very many poor and needy instead of rich. Men infinite in number, driven by wine, have committed unjust and impious murders. Very many cities, long besieged and not taken, when their guards were buried in sleep and wine, have been laid open to the enemy and burnt up in fires. There are also many other unspeakable and innumerable things by which, through the vices of drunkenness, this world has long been frequently troubled, and is troubled now: and if I wished to bring forward from the Lord's books or from secular books, for each of these, examples and the persons through whom these things were done, the enormous size of the book would bring weariness to the readers.

Yet we in this work made our beginning of reproach and admonition with priests and levites for this reason, so that we should not seem perhaps to make clerics or ministers of God exempt from this infection, by which, through the Lord's rebuke, we confound all who are given to this vice: for it befits them all the more, since they teach the people to abstain from various faults, to take care with cautious watchfulness that they do not fall into any vice or fault; and the Apostle rebukes them with just reproof, saying: But do you suppose, O man, who judge those who do such things and do them yourself, that you will escape the judgement of God? Likewise: You who teach another, do not teach yourself; you who abhor idols, commit sacrilege (Rom. 2:3, 21 and 22): and the rest, by which he reproves those who do not themselves abstain from the vices they forbid; and in what they judge others, they condemn themselves. Therefore we urge all clerics, and laymen placed in various dignities of this kind, to read this little book over frequently: so that when anyone has advanced, pleasing to God, in good conduct and sobriety, he may always rejoice gladly in the Lord God at our rebuke, giving thanks to God through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
PREFATORY NOTE TO THE BOOK ON TRUE AND FALSE PENANCE.

Almost this whole book was taken over under the name of Augustine into the Decretum by Gratian, and into the Sentences by Peter Lombard. Afterwards Peter of Blois cited it and attributed it to Augustine in his books On Confession and On Penance, as did Vincent of Beauvais in the Moral Mirror, book 3, part 10, distinction 2; Thomas Aquinas in the Summa Theologica; and others after them. Trithemius, however, in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, believes it spurious, because, he says, in chapter 17 Augustine himself is cited. Martin Navarrus objects, in volume 2, Commentary on distinction 5 On Penance, and says it should rather be supposed that the passage in which Augustine is cited migrated into the text from a note written in the margin by some learned man, than that it should for that reason be denied that this excellent book, attributed to him for so many centuries, is Augustine's. Navarrus's conjecture is supported by old manuscripts we have inspected, which at that place at least omit the name of Augustine: yet the sense requires it, and Gratian in fact reads it. But whatever is finally thought of this passage, other arguments abound on every side which loudly declare that this work is not Augustine's. Some were collected by Bernard Vindingus in the Augustinian Critic, and set against a certain recent theologian, as he puts it, not a bad one otherwise, who contended that in style and doctrine it was wholly Augustinian, and so that it had been foolishly denied to him by Erasmus and other leaders: namely phrases foreign to Augustine, in chapter 5: Naaman lost his leprosy through water. Chapter 4: Peter denied the Lord, and excommunicated the friends of Christ from himself. Likewise chapters 4, 6 and 7: To promise punishment. Chapter 9: To be anxious toward God. In the same place: Let him confess to a better [priest] than he can. Chapter 17: The sinner must bear fruit in penance. In expounding the Scriptures he shows that the author has neither Augustine's skill nor agreement with him. For in chapter 5 he says: That he promised forgiveness to all, he declares by other promises: "Whoever confesses me before men," that is, every sinner, however great and however often, of whatever order, even if he be a priest, "I too will confess him before my Father." Chapter 9: He healed the whole man on the sabbath, because he freed both the body from infirmity and the soul from all contagion. Chapter 11: In Peter and John and James and the father and mother of the girl (Luke 8:51) the priests of the Church are figuratively contained. By the tears of the widowed mother, of Martha and Mary and of the crowd of Jews, we are taught, he says, that for those sinning publicly not their own merit but that of the Church suffices, etc. Chapter 14: All this variety must be confessed: if he sinned in a sacred place, or [against one] to whom he owed excellence of faith, as are the houses of lords and of many others; if at a time set for prayer, or on a feast of the saints, and in a time of fasting, etc. If anyone falls into avarice, he has also diminished chastity. Besides, it is suggested in chapter 6 that every good person before Christ's coming was held in the underworld, while Augustine, in book 12 of On Genesis according to the Letter, chapters 33 and 34, disagrees on this matter or at least is doubtful; and in chapter 8 the Acts of Saint Andrew are mentioned, which according to the learned were made public long after Augustine.

We have corrected the book against the manuscripts of the Augustinians of the great convent of Paris, against the Cistercian one, against the Vatican one, and also against the collections of Gratian and Lombard. In the manuscripts it is entitled On True and False Penance; [the words] 'to a devoted [woman] of Christ' are omitted. And at the end they have: Here ends On Confession.
